recent_posts.author: SalmanDev
recent_posts.content_text: @Hanssen I have a question on the Time Lock + Cheque suggestion. Per RFC 0039 (rule 1.b.ii), when the receiver claims a Cheque cell, the cell’s capacity must go back to the sender, so for plain CKB the recipient would receive nothing. I also confirmed it with a test (error 8). Cheque looks designed for typed assets such as UDTs, where the receiver gets the token. How did you picture combining the two locks for native CKB?

recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
We filled one Fiber LSP to 11,496 channels on a local CKB dev chain, with the build and config that our testnet LSP, the one behind the Cellula wallet, ran that day. A payment between two wallets still took 4 to 5 s, as it did with 350 channels.
The channel count turned out not to be the limit. What sizes an LSP is how many wallets are awake at the same moment and how fast it can open channels. Below: how we tested, the numbers, what we changed on the way, and what we would run.
Why we asked
The Cellula wallet pays over Fiber from a browser or a phone, with no node to run. Each wallet’s channel is held at an LSP, a Fiber node that serves many wallets, while the channel keys stay on the device and sign in the wallet’s own signer.
So anyone running an LSP needs to know how many wallets one can carry. Our first estimate, before testing, was 10 to 20 LSPs of about 1,000 channels for 10,000 wallets. A testnet faucet cannot fund 10,000 channels, so we tested on a dev chain instead.
How we tested
Everything that touches the chain matched testnet; only the chain itself was local.
Chain: ckb 0.210.0 with Fiber’s dev spec. Testnet’s ckb-auth, FundingLock and CommitmentLock copied byte for byte and deployed by type id.
LSP: the binary and config.yml of our testnet LSP, with only paths, ports, keys and the chain changed, and up to 1,500 wallets awake instead of 600 in the 8-core runs. Its own CKB node beside it. LSP support comes from nervosnetwork/fiber#1623.
Cores: fnn held to 4 cores for the fill. Then the CKB node, fnn and our gateway held to 8 cores together, as one 8-vCPU server would run them.
Wallets: test wallets on a PC, ten to a Node process, each with its own key and the wallet’s signer built for the dev chain.
Blocks: every 8 s to measure the opening rate, every 2 s to fill faster.
The fill ran on 2026-10-28. The 11,496 column was measured on 2026-10-29, except the watchtower round, read the evening before at the same count.
What one LSP held
One LSP took every channel we gave it, and payment time barely moved with the count.
image3200×1800 383 KB
Measure
9,988 channels, 4 cores
11,496 channels, 8 cores
One payment, two fresh wallets
3.8 s
3.9, 3.9 and 5.0 s
Ten pairs paying at once, p50
6.4 to 7.7 s
5.4 to 13.0 s
Wallets awake at the same moment
not measured
1,420, all served
Restart, until every channel is ready
55 s
68 s
CPU at rest
4 to 6% of one core
7% of one core
Memory after a restart
5.8 GB
6.0 GB
Watchtower round, one core every 10 min
142 s
99 to 117 s
The day before, at 10,698 channels on 8 cores, 1,500 of 1,500 wallets woke. At 11,496 our harness started 1,420: the rest could not reach the one CKB node all test wallets share, and never reached the LSP. Every wallet that started woke, and in both runs the 50 pairs among them paid.
Openings, with 8 s blocks: 40 a minute early in the fill, 61 a minute past 10,000 channels on 8 cores. For comparison, one payment took 3.8 to 4.8 s at 350 channels.
What we changed on the way
Four changes came out of the test, each measured before and after on the same chain.
A tenant registry index in fnn. Finding a tenant by key, or counting tenants, read and deserialized every tenant record on the service actor; registering one tenant did it four times. Now an index is built once from the store, and lsp_get_status answers in 0.6 ms with 10,754 tenants. With 1,500 wallets waking at once, the pairs that paid went from 34 to 50 of 50 and the LSP’s memory from 9.2 to 5.6 GB; waves of 400 openings stopped timing out. Offered upstream as chenyukang/fiber#9, into the LSP support branch.
One shared tenant list in our gateway. A dozen readers each fetched the full list, 4.5 MB at 10,754 tenants. Now they share one copy at most 15 s old.
A faster signer for long histories. The signer stopped decoding its whole state on every request: ten long-history wallets paying one, 128.7 s before, 22.2 s after, the same as fresh wallets.
A smaller signing state. It grew about 14 KB a payment, mostly a recovery record per commitment. In our tests the commitment lock took the newest revocation for any older commitment of the same lane, so the signer now keeps nothing below it. A state after 96 payments went from 1.31 MB to 130 KB, and to about 16 KB with a second pass over settled payments.
The signer changes are live in the Cellula wallet on testnet. We asked the Fiber team on #1623 whether they read the revocation rule the same way. Two other fixes from running this LSP are merged in Fiber: #1703 and #1708.
Sizing an LSP
Eight cores carried 11,496 channels with 1,420 wallets awake at once, the CKB node and our gateway included. We would run two for availability, each on its own CKB node.
What sets the size, in the order we hit it:
Wallets awake at once. max_active_tenants caps it; our testnet LSP runs 600. Waking 1,000 wallets at once kept about 7 cores busy for two minutes.
Opening rate. 40 to 61 channels a minute. Waves of 100 openings were always clean.
The watchtower round. One core, every 10 minutes: 1.8 s at 290 channels, 45 s at 5,000, 99 to 142 s from 9,988 to 11,496.
Memory. fnn holds about 6 GB at rest with 11,496 channels, and 6.5 to 8.6 GB with about 1,400 wallets awake. It peaked at 13.5 GB while opening 10,000 channels back to back, so size RAM for the peak.
What’s next
We want to run this on CKB mainnet: a public LSP that any wallet signing with Fiber’s LSP SDK can use, with the signer changes offered to that SDK. Before we put it to the Community Fund DAO, we would like to hear from the Fiber team and from anyone building a wallet on Fiber.
Talk to us
These numbers come from a copy of the LSP behind the Cellula wallet on testnet. Building an LSP or a wallet on Fiber? Reply here, or find us at cellula.id and t.me/cellula_id. Thanks to the Fiber team for fnn and the LSP support this is built on.

Great work! 11.5k channels on a single LSP is pretty encouraging, especially with the optimisations you found along the way.
Would be interesting to see some sustained concurrent payment tests across separate LSPs next, just to get a better feel for real-world scaling.
Also i noticed the watchtower takes around 100s per scan at this scale. Curious whether that’s mainly database reads/scanning or CKB indexer/RPC overhead. Might be a good next optimisation target.
Really nice progress.

Hi @Dorex45, thanks for checking in. To clarify the payment schedule, the approved proposal lists three milestones at $1,000 each and does not include a request for an upfront payment.
We will follow the milestone-based payment process: once a milestone is completed, please publish a completion report with supporting evidence on Nervos Talk. This is followed by a two-week community review. After that review, if the community has no further concerns that the milestone has been delivered, the committee will arrange the corresponding payment.
In other words, the passing vote approves the proposal and its budget; it does not trigger an upfront release of the full $3,000. The next payment step is therefore the Milestone 1 completion report.
I hope this clarifies the timeline and helps with your planning.

topics.title: Spark Program | CellFlow — Durable CCC Transaction Recovery PoC

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CellFlow — Durable CCC Transaction Recovery PoC
recent_posts.author: Dangbaty2004
recent_posts.content_text:
Capture1906×878 147 KB
Applicant: Dang Ba Ty
Discord: tyforwork
Email: dangbaty.work@gmail.com
GitHub: tydeptrai21042004 (Dang Ba Ty) · GitHub
Funding requested: $500 USD, payable in equivalent CKB
Duration: 4 weeks
Project type: CKB Developer Infrastructure / Proof of Concept
Project links:
Repository: GitHub - tydeptrai21042004/CellFlow · GitHub
Live application: https://cellflow-brown.vercel.app/
Interactive demo: CellFlow Demo — Transaction Recovery Walkthrough
CKBuilder technical review: CellFlow: durable CKB transaction operations and recovery for applications · Issue #38 · Nervos-Community-Catalyst/CKBuilder-projects · GitHub
1. Project Overview
CellFlow explores whether a CKB application can safely recover an uncertain transaction after a backend restart and finalize its business operation exactly once, using CCC, PostgreSQL, and independently verifiable CKB chain evidence.
Consider a transaction accepted by a CKB node whose broadcast response is lost. The application cannot safely conclude that the transaction failed. Similarly, receiving a later confirmation is insufficient to prove that every required output Cell assertion has been verified.
CellFlow already implements a recovery and settlement model addressing these failure conditions.
For this Spark proposal, I want to create a small end-to-end CCC reference application demonstrating the model with persistent PostgreSQL state, real CKB Testnet transactions, controlled failure injection, and application-level settlement.
The central question is:
Can another CKB developer integrate CellFlow into a real CCC workflow and recover an uncertain transaction safely, without implementing their own durable transaction-reconciliation system?
The objective is to answer this question through one focused, reproducible experiment rather than expand CellFlow into a larger platform.
2. Applicant Background and Contact
I am Dang Ba Ty, the primary developer of CellFlow, and have been developing CKB-related applications and developer tools through the CKBuilder program.
CellFlow has received technical feedback from CKB community developers, including @alesfer001 and @Xcodes-chain, covering RBF, input conflicts, multiple transaction attempts, settlement assertions, reorg monitoring, and reproducible evidence.
I have incorporated the main architectural corrections into the implementation. The October 28 follow-up review confirmed that the earlier premature-settlement concern had been addressed in the reviewed source paths.
The remaining challenge is demonstrating complete application integration under independently reproducible conditions.
Contact information:
Discord: tyforwork
Email: dangbaty.work@gmail.com
GitHub: tydeptrai21042004 (Dang Ba Ty) · GitHub
I will be responsible for the CCC integration, PostgreSQL validation, Testnet experiments, documentation, and final report.
3. Problem and Motivation
CCC provides transaction construction and signing, while CKB RPC provides information about transaction and chain state.
However, an application must still decide what to do when a signed transaction has been submitted but its outcome is uncertain.
Consider this scenario:
A user signs a CKB transaction through CCC.
The backend persists the transaction identity and broadcasts it.
The CKB node accepts the transaction.
The successful RPC response is lost.
The application worker restarts.
The application must determine whether the original transaction committed before retrying or finalizing anything.
A second failure can occur after confirmation: the expected output Cell may not yet be verifiable because an RPC query is temporarily unavailable.
Treating either uncertainty as success may cause premature business effects. Treating a lost response as definitive failure can lead to unsafe retries.
These are practical operational problems for applications that integrate CKB transactions with persistent business state.
I developed CellFlow to make these failure boundaries explicit. The next step is to determine whether the resulting integration is practical and reusable for other CKB developers.
4. Proposed Solution
I propose building a minimal reference application demonstrating the complete lifecycle of a real CKB Testnet transaction.
The application will:
Connect a CCC-compatible wallet.
Construct and sign a real CKB Testnet transaction.
Persist the business intent, transaction identity, input references, and signed-payload fingerprint in PostgreSQL before broadcast.
Broadcast the signed transaction through CKB RPC.
Intentionally discard a successful broadcast response in a controlled fault-injection scenario.
Preserve the uncertain submission state.
Restart the application worker and recover the operation from PostgreSQL.
Reconcile the transaction against canonical CKB state.
Verify the configured confirmation policy and expected Cell assertions.
Emit intent.settlement_ready only when all required conditions are satisfied.
Finalize the application’s business operation idempotently, without duplicate execution.
Database Responsibilities
The PoC will demonstrate two logically separate persistence responsibilities using an isolated PostgreSQL instance.
A. CellFlow Operational Database
Stores:
business intents and transaction attempts;
transaction hashes and input references;
submission, chain, and workflow states;
reconciliation events and confirmation evidence;
expected-Cell assertions;
settlement and revocation events;
webhook delivery and idempotency records.
B. Reference Application Database
Stores a small application-level business operation that is finalized only after a verified settlement-ready event.
Duplicate events must not apply the same business effect twice.
CKB remains authoritative for transaction confirmation and Cell liveness. PostgreSQL preserves operational history and the application state needed to recover safely across restarts.
5. Technical Architecture
Technology stack:
TypeScript / Node.js
CKB CCC
CKB Testnet JSON-RPC
PostgreSQL
Existing CellFlow recovery and settlement engine
Next.js reference interface
Proposed Workflow
flowchart TD
A["Connect CCC wallet"] --> B["Build and sign Testnet transaction"]
B --> C["Persist intent and signed attempt"]
C --> D[("PostgreSQL: CellFlow operational state")]
D --> E["Broadcast through CKB RPC"]
E --> F["Inject lost RPC response"]
F --> G["SUBMISSION_UNKNOWN"]
G --> H["Restart backend worker"]
H --> I["Recover persisted intent"]
I --> J["Reconcile canonical CKB state"]
J --> K{"Confirmation policy and required Cell assertions pass?"}
K -->|No| L["Remain unsettled and retry observation"]
L --> J
K -->|Yes| M["intent.settlement_ready"]
M --> N["Finalize business effect idempotently"]
N --> O[("PostgreSQL: application business state")]
Core Safety Properties
Wallet signing remains outside CellFlow; private keys are never stored by the service.
Backend API credentials are not exposed to the browser.
A lost broadcast response does not trigger an automatic blind rebroadcast.
A pending or unavailable required Cell assertion prevents settlement readiness.
Repeated callbacks or retries cannot finalize the same business operation twice.
Confirmation depth is treated as a policy, not an absolute finality guarantee.
Fault injection is labeled separately from observed CKB network events.
The PoC will reuse CellFlow’s existing recovery engine instead of introducing a second transaction state machine.
6. Current State vs. Funded Work
Already Implemented
The existing CellFlow repository includes:
durable transaction intents and multiple transaction attempts;
PostgreSQL schema, migrations, and persistence repositories;
CCC preparation and tracking utilities;
lost-response and RBF recovery logic;
expected-Cell verification;
settlement-ready and settlement-revoked events;
webhook delivery infrastructure;
automated regression tests;
author-reported real Testnet recovery and RBF experiments;
a hosted operator interface and separate interactive simulation.
These features form the existing technical foundation and are not being requested for retroactive funding.
New Work Proposed for Spark
The funding will support combining and validating these components in a new, independently usable reference integration.
The specific new contribution is:
A minimal CCC reference application using the real CellFlow API.
Reproducible PostgreSQL setup covering both operational and application state.
A complete CKB Testnet recovery exercise including lost-response injection and worker restart.
Database-backed verification that business finalization occurs exactly once.
A reproducible evidence package tied to the tested source revision.
External developer feedback on integration difficulty and usefulness.
The goal is to validate integration usability and operational correctness, not expand the existing backend feature set.
7. Execution Plan and Milestones

1. Project Overview

CellFlow explores whether a CKB application can safely recover an uncertain transaction after a backend restart and finalize its business operation exactly once, using CCC, PostgreSQL, and independently verifiable CKB chain evidence.

Consider a transaction accepted by a CKB node whose broadcast response is lost. The application cannot safely conclude that the transaction failed. Similarly, receiving a later confirmation is insufficient to prove that every required output Cell assertion has been verified.

CellFlow already implements a recovery and settlement model addressing these failure conditions.

For this Spark proposal, I want to create a small end-to-end CCC reference application demonstrating the model with persistent PostgreSQL state, real CKB Testnet transactions, controlled failure injection, and application-level settlement.

The central question is:

Can another CKB developer integrate CellFlow into a real CCC workflow and recover an uncertain transaction safely, without implementing their own durable transaction-reconciliation system?

The objective is to answer this question through one focused, reproducible experiment rather than expand CellFlow into a larger platform.

2. Applicant Background and Contact

I am Dang Ba Ty, the primary developer of CellFlow, and have been developing CKB-related applications and developer tools through the CKBuilder program.

CellFlow has received technical feedback from CKB community developers, including @alesfer001 and @Xcodes-chain, covering RBF, input conflicts, multiple transaction attempts, settlement assertions, reorg monitoring, and reproducible evidence.

I have incorporated the main architectural corrections into the implementation. The October 28 follow-up review confirmed that the earlier premature-settlement concern had been addressed in the reviewed source paths.

The remaining challenge is demonstrating complete application integration under independently reproducible conditions.

Contact information:

  • Discord: tyforwork

  • Email: dangbaty.work@gmail.com

  • GitHub: tydeptrai21042004 (Dang Ba Ty) · GitHub

I will be responsible for the CCC integration, PostgreSQL validation, Testnet experiments, documentation, and final report.

3. Problem and Motivation

CCC provides transaction construction and signing, while CKB RPC provides information about transaction and chain state.

However, an application must still decide what to do when a signed transaction has been submitted but its outcome is uncertain.

Consider this scenario:

  1. A user signs a CKB transaction through CCC.

  2. The backend persists the transaction identity and broadcasts it.

  3. The CKB node accepts the transaction.

  4. The successful RPC response is lost.

  5. The application worker restarts.

  6. The application must determine whether the original transaction committed before retrying or finalizing anything.

A second failure can occur after confirmation: the expected output Cell may not yet be verifiable because an RPC query is temporarily unavailable.

Treating either uncertainty as success may cause premature business effects. Treating a lost response as definitive failure can lead to unsafe retries.

These are practical operational problems for applications that integrate CKB transactions with persistent business state.

I developed CellFlow to make these failure boundaries explicit. The next step is to determine whether the resulting integration is practical and reusable for other CKB developers.

4. Proposed Solution

I propose building a minimal reference application demonstrating the complete lifecycle of a real CKB Testnet transaction.

The application will:

  1. Connect a CCC-compatible wallet.

  2. Construct and sign a real CKB Testnet transaction.

  3. Persist the business intent, transaction identity, input references, and signed-payload fingerprint in PostgreSQL before broadcast.

  4. Broadcast the signed transaction through CKB RPC.

  5. Intentionally discard a successful broadcast response in a controlled fault-injection scenario.

  6. Preserve the uncertain submission state.

  7. Restart the application worker and recover the operation from PostgreSQL.

  8. Reconcile the transaction against canonical CKB state.

  9. Verify the configured confirmation policy and expected Cell assertions.

  10. Emit intent.settlement_ready only when all required conditions are satisfied.

  11. Finalize the application’s business operation idempotently, without duplicate execution.

Database Responsibilities

The PoC will demonstrate two logically separate persistence responsibilities using an isolated PostgreSQL instance.

A. CellFlow Operational Database

Stores:

  • business intents and transaction attempts;

  • transaction hashes and input references;

  • submission, chain, and workflow states;

  • reconciliation events and confirmation evidence;

  • expected-Cell assertions;

  • settlement and revocation events;

  • webhook delivery and idempotency records.

B. Reference Application Database

Stores a small application-level business operation that is finalized only after a verified settlement-ready event.

Duplicate events must not apply the same business effect twice.

CKB remains authoritative for transaction confirmation and Cell liveness. PostgreSQL preserves operational history and the application state needed to recover safely across restarts.

5. Technical Architecture

Technology stack:

  • TypeScript / Node.js

  • CKB CCC

  • CKB Testnet JSON-RPC

  • PostgreSQL

  • Existing CellFlow recovery and settlement engine

  • Next.js reference interface

flowchart TD

    B --> C["Persist intent and signed attempt"]
    C --> D[("PostgreSQL: CellFlow operational state")]

    E --> F["Inject lost RPC response"]

    G --> H["Restart backend worker"]
    H --> I["Recover persisted intent"]
    I --> J["Reconcile canonical CKB state"]
    J --> K{"Confirmation policy and required Cell assertions pass?"}
    K -->|No| L["Remain unsettled and retry observation"]
    L --> J
    K -->|Yes| M["intent.settlement_ready"]
    M --> N["Finalize business effect idempotently"]
    N --> O[("PostgreSQL: application business state")]

Core Safety Properties

  • Wallet signing remains outside CellFlow; private keys are never stored by the service.

  • Backend API credentials are not exposed to the browser.

  • A lost broadcast response does not trigger an automatic blind rebroadcast.

  • A pending or unavailable required Cell assertion prevents settlement readiness.

  • Repeated callbacks or retries cannot finalize the same business operation twice.

  • Confirmation depth is treated as a policy, not an absolute finality guarantee.

  • Fault injection is labeled separately from observed CKB network events.

The PoC will reuse CellFlow’s existing recovery engine instead of introducing a second transaction state machine.

1. Project overview
Purpose: Build on a browser light-client prototype that has completed a real testnet transfer to improve stability, implement mainnet transfers and full Nervos DAO deposits and withdrawals, and deliver a reusable kit for other dApps.
Request: USD 1,000 equivalent in CKB over four weeks, delivered through two milestones under the MIT license.
Scope: Desktop Chrome and Firefox, existing CCC wallet connections, mainnet and testnet. The application does not hold private keys; wallets approve and sign transactions.
2. Team profile
Applicant and maintainer: Akane; GitHub: Akane-CN; Nervos Talk: Akane.
Email: akane@random-walk.co.jp.
Repository: GitHub - Akane-CN/light-dapp-kit · GitHub
3. Project background
CKB already provides a browser-capable WASM light client as a foundation for client-side verification. This project focuses on sustained operation during asset management, including synchronization, reconnection, local persistence and transaction confirmation.
Users need balances and asset operations to remain reliable after a page reload or a network interruption. Developers need those capabilities in reusable components rather than repeatedly diagnosing the same underlying failures.
4. Solution
Browser-resident, verifiable data access: Run chain queries and light-client validation in the user’s browser to reduce dependence on remote RPC data services. Applications receive a consistent interface to locally verified data, while users can see synchronization, data completeness and transaction progress.
Real asset workflows as the engineering workload: Implement mainnet transfers and the full DAO deposit, withdrawal-request and unlock sequence to exercise historical queries, persistent state and multi-stage transactions. Use the failures encountered in these workflows to improve synchronization, reconnection, storage and recovery across the complete user experience.
Improvements that other applications can reuse: Improve and release the existing core adapter, React APIs, project template and reference application together with reproductions, regression tests and optimization findings. Submit reusable underlying fixes upstream so the benefits extend beyond this application.
5. Technical approach and primary risk
Stack: Use the official CKB WASM light client, CCC, TypeScript, Bun, Vite and React. CCC handles transaction construction and wallet signing; the browser light client supplies chain data, broadcasts transactions and tracks confirmation.
Primary risk and response: Browser light-client stability is the main engineering risk, with testing focused on stalled synchronization, reconnection, Worker lifecycle and IndexedDB behavior. Diagnose encountered failures, implement targeted fixes or optimizations, and retain before/after measurements, regression cases and unresolved issues.
Correctness: Track header synchronization separately from address scanning so partial data is not presented as a complete balance. Isolate mainnet/testnet configuration and storage, and verify the historical headers, dependencies and unlock conditions required by DAO transactions.
Network boundary: Kit-controlled chain queries, broadcast and confirmation must not use remote node/indexer RPC or hidden fallbacks. Static assets, P2P connections and wallet-owned traffic are documented separately.
6. Execution plan
M1: browser stability and basic transactions, weeks 1-2
Week 1: Extend the existing Chromium tests with synchronization, memory, storage and reconnection baselines; reproduce priority issues and identify existing DAO deposits suitable for withdrawal verification within the project window.
Week 2: Fix or optimize priority issues, add DAO transaction construction and extend the existing testnet transfer flow with failure-recovery regressions. Deliver reproductions, before/after results and a runnable revision.
M2: mainnet asset workflows and reusable release, weeks 3-4
Week 3: Complete mainnet transfers, DAO deposits, withdrawal requests and eligible unlocks, including wallet interaction, status display and failure recovery.
Week 4: Finish both-browser stability tests, independent-project integration and mainnet acceptance; publish the packages, reference app, documentation and walkthrough.
7. Funding by deliverable
USD 400: Browser light-client stability diagnosis, fixes and performance optimization.
USD 300: Mainnet transfer and DAO deposit/withdrawal implementation and verification.
USD 300: Component and reference-app improvements, packaging, tests and integration documentation.
Total: USD 1,000.
Payment schedule: USD 200 at launch, USD 400 after M1 acceptance and USD 400 after M2 acceptance.
8. Deliverables and verification
Stability improvements: Run each target browser continuously for at least two hours and verify recovery after disconnection, reload and reopening. Provide synchronization timings, memory trends, reproductions and before/after results, with the required workflows actually passing.
Mainnet functionality: Publish confirmed transaction hashes for a transfer, DAO deposit, withdrawal request and unlocked withdrawal, with the corresponding balance and Cell changes. Each transaction is approved and signed in the connected test wallet; testnet covers regression and failure scenarios.
DAO verification: M1 selects existing deposits eligible for unlocking within the project window; M2 verifies new deposits, withdrawal requests and unlocks separately.
Packages and evidence: Generate an application in a clean directory, integrate the packages into a separate CCC project and repeat core workflows with remote chain-data RPC blocked, including Workers and service workers. Deliver sanitized logs, pinned versions, replay instructions, the integration guide and walkthrough video.
9. Current state vs. funded work
Existing implementation: The public repository includes the core adapter, React Provider and hooks, an application generator, and balance, transfer and read-only DAO pages.
Execution evidence: A passing Chromium browser test used a test signer to complete a real 100 CKB testnet self-transfer and wait for on-chain confirmation. Type checking, builds and unit tests passed on the same revision.
Optimization baseline: The current code includes targeted handling of synchronization state and address-scan start points, with recorded synchronization and confirmation timings to guide further improvements.
Funded additions: Improve browser stability, complete mainnet and DAO deposit/withdrawal workflows, verify compatibility with real wallets, and publish reusable releases based on the existing prototype.
10. CKB alignment
The project brings CKB light-client verification, the Cell model and Nervos DAO asset workflows into browser applications. Real mainnet use will guide stability improvements, with open-source components and fixes expanding the options for applications that avoid dependence on remote chain-data services.

  • Browser-resident, verifiable data access: Run chain queries and light-client validation in the user’s browser to reduce dependence on remote RPC data services. Applications receive a consistent interface to locally verified data, while users can see synchronization, data completeness and transaction progress.
  • Real asset workflows as the engineering workload: Implement mainnet transfers and the full DAO deposit, withdrawal-request and unlock sequence to exercise historical queries, persistent state and multi-stage transactions. Use the failures encountered in these workflows to improve synchronization, reconnection, storage and recovery across the complete user experience.
  • Improvements that other applications can reuse: Improve and release the existing core adapter, React APIs, project template and reference application together with reproductions, regression tests and optimization findings. Submit reusable underlying fixes upstream so the benefits extend beyond this application.

5. Technical approach and primary risk

  • Stack: Use the official CKB WASM light client, CCC, TypeScript, Bun, Vite and React. CCC handles transaction construction and wallet signing; the browser light client supplies chain data, broadcasts transactions and tracks confirmation.
  • Primary risk and response: Browser light-client stability is the main engineering risk, with testing focused on stalled synchronization, reconnection, Worker lifecycle and IndexedDB behavior. Diagnose encountered failures, implement targeted fixes or optimizations, and retain before/after measurements, regression cases and unresolved issues.
  • Correctness: Track header synchronization separately from address scanning so partial data is not presented as a complete balance. Isolate mainnet/testnet configuration and storage, and verify the historical headers, dependencies and unlock conditions required by DAO transactions.
  • Network boundary: Kit-controlled chain queries, broadcast and confirmation must not use remote node/indexer RPC or hidden fallbacks. Static assets, P2P connections and wallet-owned traffic are documented separately.

  • Week 2: Fix or optimize priority issues, add DAO transaction construction and extend the existing testnet transfer flow with failure-recovery regressions. Deliver reproductions, before/after results and a runnable revision.

M2: mainnet asset workflows and reusable release, weeks 3-4

  • Week 3: Complete mainnet transfers, DAO deposits, withdrawal requests and eligible unlocks, including wallet interaction, status display and failure recovery.
  • Week 4: Finish both-browser stability tests, independent-project integration and mainnet acceptance; publish the packages, reference app, documentation and walkthrough.
